cues.text: Electric fans, toy cars, power drills, even the wipers on a car, all spin because of a small and clever machine: the DC motor.
cues.say: Electric fans, toy cars, power drills, even the wipers on a car, all spin because of a small and clever machine: the D C motor.

cues.text: In this video, you'll see exactly how it turns electricity into rotation, one step at a time.
Let's start with the parts.
Two permanent magnets, one north and one south, make up the stator. They stay still, and create a magnetic field in the gap between them.
In the middle is a rectangular coil of wire, called the armature. It is mounted on a shaft, so it is free to rotate.
At the end of the shaft sits the commutator, a ring split into two halves.
Two carbon brushes press against the commutator, and connect it to the battery.
Between the magnets there is a magnetic field.
By convention, the field lines run from the north pole to the south pole, here from left to right.
The stronger the magnets, the stronger the field.
Now connect the battery, so that current flows through the coil.
On the right-hand side, the current comes out of the screen, drawn as a dot.
A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force, and its direction comes from Fleming's left-hand rule.
First finger for the field, second finger for the current, and the thumb gives the force: upward here.
On the left, the current goes into the screen, drawn as a cross, so the force is downward.
The size of the force is B times I times L: field strength, current, and length of wire.
These two forces are equal and opposite, but they act on opposite sides of the axle.
Together they create a turning effect called torque, and the coil begins to rotate.
More current, a stronger field, or more turns of wire all give a bigger torque.
But there is a problem.
When the coil reaches the vertical position, the forces now act along the coil, instead of across it, so the torque drops to zero.
If the current kept flowing the same way, the coil would overshoot, get pulled back, and simply stop here.
That is the job of the commutator.
As the coil swings past the vertical, each half of the split ring moves from one brush to the other.
This reverses the current in the coil at exactly the right moment.
As a result, the side on the right always carries current out of the screen, so it is always pushed upward, and the coil keeps turning the same way.
Once the coil spins, something interesting happens.
A conductor moving through a magnetic field generates its own voltage, called back EMF, which opposes the battery.
cues.say: A conductor moving through a magnetic field generates its own voltage, called back E M F, which opposes the battery.

cues.text: As the motor speeds up, the back EMF grows, the current falls, and the speed settles at a steady value.
cues.say: As the motor speeds up, the back E M F grows, the current falls, and the speed settles at a steady value.

cues.text: That is why a motor draws a large current when it starts, and much less when it is running.
Real motors use many coils, set at different angles, with a commutator of many segments, for smooth and steady torque.
To recap: current in a magnetic field produces a force.
Two opposite forces produce torque.
And the commutator keeps that torque turning the same way.
